notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Numbers 10, drawn from the sources I was able to access:

---

## Numbers 10:1–10 — The Two Silver Trumpets

**v. 1:** The command to make silver trumpets closes out the first major section of Numbers (chapters 1–10), the preparation at Sinai before the march. The trumpets regulation is placed here because one primary use was connected with the order of march (Pulpit). The preceptaustin.org site notes that these verses “signal bringing the first major portion of Numbers to a close,” part of putting all things in place for ritual ceremonies and worship prior to the journey (Nu 7:1–10:10).
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-10-commentary
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/10.htm

**v. 2:** “Make two trumpets of silver, of hammered work.” The Hebrew word is *ḥăṣōṣrāh*, a straight metal trumpet distinct from the curved ram’s horn *shophar*. Josephus describes them as about 18 inches (45 cm) long with a flared opening at the end; they are depicted on the Arch of Titus in Rome. They were made of a single silver plate beaten into shape (*mikshah*). The two trumpets were used for “calling the congregation” (assembly) and “directing the movement of the camps” (marching). Guzik notes that before Israel could obey God, they first had to give Him their attention – the trumpets served that purpose.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-10/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/10.htm

**v. 3:** When both trumpets were blown together, the whole congregation assembled at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. Gill explains that this even, continued sound on both trumpets was the signal for a general assembly at the tabernacle door, the usual place of meeting where the Lord met them (cf. Ex 29:42).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-10.html

**v. 4:** “If only one is sounded, then the leaders… are to gather before you.” Ellicott notes an alternative translation: “but once” or “at the same time” – meaning a single, uniform blast rather than a continuous one. The signal distinguished between summoning the whole congregation (both trumpets) and summoning only the princes (one trumpet or a distinct blast).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm

**v. 5:** “When you sound short blasts, the camps that lie on the east side are to set out.” The Hebrew word *teruah* (“alarm”) is thought to denote a loud, staccato or continuous peal, easily distinguished from the longer, smoother blasts for assembly. Jewish tradition holds that long blasts assembled the people; short staccato blasts signaled movement or battle (Wenham, cited by Guzik). MacArthur adds that Jewish tradition described the advance signal as a succession of three shorter notes.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-10/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-10-commentary
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm

**v. 6:** A second alarm signaled the south-side camps (Reuben, Simeon, Gad) to set out. The text only mentions two alarms, but the Septuagint (LXX) inserts instructions for a third alarm for the western camps and a fourth for the northern camps. Ellicott and JFB both note this LXX addition. JFB comments: “Thus the greatest order and discipline were established in the Israelitish camp – no military march could be better regulated.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/numbers/10.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/10.htm

**v. 7:** “To convene the assembly, you are to sound long blasts, not short ones.” A clear, intelligible distinction between the summons to gather and the signal to march was essential. Ellicott draws a New Testament parallel: “So the gospel trumpet must at no time give an uncertain sound (1 Corinthians 14:8), but must be used faithfully and diligently by the spiritual watchmen.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm

**v. 8:** “The sons of Aaron, the priests, are to sound the trumpets. This shall be a permanent statute for you.” Since Aaron had only two sons at this time (Eleazar and Ithamar), two trumpets sufficed. The Pulpit Commentary notes that this “ordinance forever” cannot be exhausted by 1,500 years of literal use followed by disuse; it must be perpetuated “forever” in the gospel, or the Divine word has failed. In Solomon’s time the number grew to 120 priests with 120 trumpets (2 Chr 5:12).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/10.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-10-commentary

**v. 9:** “When you enter into battle… sound short blasts on the trumpets, and you will be remembered before the LORD your God and saved from your enemies.” The trumpets were a call to God to remember His covenant promises and act. Gill notes that the alarm was meant to break hearts, bring repentance, and cause the people to cry to the Lord. The sound “made a man’s heart shake and tremble” (cf. Amos 3:6). Phinehas carried these trumpets into battle against Midian (Num 31:6), and Abijah appealed to them before battle against Jeroboam (2 Chr 13:12–14).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-10.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm

**v. 10:** Trumpets were also blown on joyous occasions, appointed feasts, and new moons, over burnt offerings and fellowship offerings. They served “as a reminder for you before your God.” Gill sees four distinct uses for the trumpets: (1) assembling the congregation, (2) signaling the march, (3) sounding alarm for war, and (4) celebrating at feasts and over sacrifices. The phrase “I am the LORD your God” seals these instructions with divine authority. Constable (cited at preceptaustin.org) notes this is the first reference to the new moon celebration in Scripture; the Jews viewed each new moon as consecrated to God in a way similar to the Sabbath.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-10.html
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-10-commentary
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-10/

**Typological reading of vv. 1–10 (shared across most Protestant traditions):** Guzik draws an extended parallel between the silver trumpets and preaching: the trumpets required effort, had to give a clear sound, gathered God’s people, led them forward, sounded an alarm for battle, proclaimed glad news, were shaped by hammering (hard impact), and were blown by called, cleansed, and consecrated priests. James Smith (cited at preceptaustin.org) sees the two trumpets as typifying the Old and New Testaments – “of a whole piece” pointing to the unity of Scripture despite different authors and times.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-10/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-10-commentary

---

## Numbers 10:11–28 — The Departure from Sinai

**v. 11:** “On the twentieth day of the second month of the second year.” Ellicott calculates that Israel had been encamped at Sinai for about 11 months and 19 days (arriving in the third month of the first year per Ex 19:1). The cloud lifted from the tabernacle for the very first time since it had been erected (Ex 40:34). The Pulpit Commentary notes the date corresponds roughly to early May, when spring verdure would still be on the land but daytime heat already intense.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/10.htm

**v. 12:** “The Israelites set out from the Wilderness of Sinai… until the cloud settled in the Wilderness of Paran.” The Pulpit Commentary explains that this is a summary statement; the actual march involved a three-day journey (v. 33) with intermediate stops before reaching Paran proper. The Wilderness of Paran (*et-Tih*) is a large limestone plateau in the northeastern Sinai, south of the Negev, described in Deut 1:19 as “that great and terrible wilderness.” It covers much of the northern Sinai peninsula.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/10.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-10/

**v. 13:** “They set out this first time according to the LORD’s command through Moses.” Guzik emphasizes that this was the first time Israel marched as an organized, prepared nation – not the disorganized mob that fled Egypt. They had been ordered (Num 1–4), cleansed (Num 5), set apart and blessed (Num 6), taught to give (Num 7–8), and reminded of deliverance (Num 9).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-10/

**vv. 14–16:** The divisions of the camp of Judah set out first, under their standard. Nahshon son of Amminadab commanded the tribe of Judah, Nethanel commanded Issachar, and Eliab commanded Zebulun. This follows the order prescribed in Numbers 2.

**v. 17:** “Then the tabernacle was taken down, and the Gershonites and the Merarites set out, transporting it.” The Pulpit Commentary notes a practical modification: In Numbers 2 the Levites were to march in the midst of the host (between the second and third divisions), but here the Gershonites and Merarites go ahead with the tabernacle fabric after Judah’s camp, so they could erect it before the Kohathites arrived with the holy objects. The Pulpit Commentary adds that this shows Divine commands “had elasticity, and left room for adaptation, under the teaching of experience, or for the sake of obvious convenience.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/10.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm

**vv. 18–20:** The camp of Reuben set out second: Elizur over Reuben, Shelumiel over Simeon, Eliasaph over Gad.

**v. 21:** “Then the Kohathites set out, transporting the holy objects; the tabernacle was to be set up before their arrival.” The Gershonites and Merarites, having gone ahead with the structural parts, would have the tabernacle erected and ready by the time the Kohathites arrived with the ark, table, lampstand, and altars.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/10.htm

**vv. 22–24:** The camp of Ephraim set out third: Elishama over Ephraim, Gamaliel over Manasseh, Abidan over Benjamin.

**vv. 25–27:** The camp of Dan set out last, serving as the rear guard. Ahiezer commanded Dan, Pagiel commanded Asher, Ahira commanded Naphtali. The Hebrew term for “rear guard” (*me’asseph*) literally means “the collector” or “gatherer” – Dan’s role was to collect stragglers and protect the rear.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/10.htm

**v. 28:** “This was the order of march for the Israelite divisions as they set out.” A summary statement closing the description.

---

## Numbers 10:29–32 — Moses and Hobab

**v. 29:** “Then Moses said to Hobab, the son of Moses’ father-in-law Reuel the Midianite…” The identity of Hobab is debated. Ellicott explains that the Hebrew word *ḥothen* can mean “father-in-law” or “brother-in-law.” Since Reuel (also called Jethro) was Moses’ father-in-law, and Judges 4:11 calls Hobab the *ḥothen* of Moses, most commentators conclude Hobab was Moses’ brother-in-law (son of Reuel/Jethro, brother of Zipporah). Moses was now over 80, so it is more probable he sought a guide of his own generation rather than the elderly Jethro. Henry’s Commentary suggests Jethro, being aged, had returned to his own land (Ex 18:27) and left his son Hobab with Moses.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-10.html

Moses’ invitation – “Come with us, and we will treat you well, for the LORD has promised good things to Israel” – expresses strong faith in God’s promise and a desire that his relatives share in the blessings. Ellicott sees this as an instructive lesson for the Church: “It is alike the duty and the privilege of all who have heard and obeyed the Gospel invitation themselves to become the instruments of its communication to others.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm

**v. 30:** Hobab initially refuses: “I will not go… I am going back to my own land and my own people.” Ellicott notes it is not expressly stated whether Hobab ultimately went with them, but Judges 1:16 confirms that the Kenites (Hobab’s descendants) did enter Canaan with the tribe of Judah, making it probable that Moses’ renewed appeal succeeded.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm

**v. 31:** “Please do not leave us… since you know where we should camp in the wilderness, and you can serve as our eyes.” Though Israel was guided by the cloud, Hobab’s practical knowledge of the desert – where to find springs, oases, and pasture – was still valuable. Ellicott notes: “Notwithstanding the direct guidance which was vouchsafed from heaven… Moses did not neglect to take advantage of all the ordinary precautions.” Guzik adds: “God’s help often comes through men like his brother-in-law Hobab.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-10/

**v. 32:** Moses promises: “If you come with us, we will share with you whatever good things the LORD gives us.” Henry’s Commentary notes two principles: (1) “We can give only what we receive” – we can do no more kindness than God enables us; (2) “Those that share with God’s Israel in their labours and hardships shall share with them in their comforts and honours.” Morgan (cited by Guzik) observes that Moses’ first appeal was to Hobab’s selfishness (“we will treat you well”), but the successful second appeal was to his usefulness (“you can be our eyes”) – the call to service and sacrifice is more forceful.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-10.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-10/

---

## Numbers 10:33–36 — The Departure Prayers of Moses

**v. 33:** “So they set out on a three-day journey from the mountain of the LORD, with the ark of the covenant of the LORD traveling ahead of them for those three days to seek a resting place for them.” Cole (cited by Guzik) notes that “three days’ journey” was common ancient Near Eastern phrasing for distance traveled by armies or caravans, averaging about 15 miles per day – so roughly 40–45 miles on this initial leg. Ellicott addresses a difficulty: Numbers 10:21 places the Kohathites (who carried the ark) in the middle of the march, yet here the ark goes ahead. He suggests the ark may not have occupied the same position in all journeys, and Ibn Ezra thought this initial three-day journey was exceptional.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-10/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm

**v. 34:** “And the cloud of the LORD was over them by day when they set out from the camp.” The cloud served both as guidance and as protection from the scorching desert sun (cf. Ps 105:39).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm

**v. 35:** “Whenever the ark set out, Moses would say: ‘Rise up, O LORD! May Your enemies be scattered; may those who hate You flee before You.’” This battle-cry prayer expresses confidence that God Himself goes before His people. Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) preached on this verse, noting its fulfillment at the cross: sin, the hosts of hell, death itself, and the gods of the heathen were all defeated and scattered. Spurgeon also applied it to church history: “When Luther first bowed his knee, the Church began to chant, ‘Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered.’ When Knox in Scotland upheld the glory of Jesus’ name… When Whitefield and Wesley, seraphic evangelists… went through this land…” The Pulpit Commentary notes that the prayers were offered by Moses, not Aaron, teaching that Israel’s marches began and ended with prayer.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-10/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/10.htm

**v. 36:** “And when it came to rest, he would say: ‘Return, O LORD, to the countless thousands of Israel.’” When the cloud stopped, Moses prayed for God’s presence to dwell among the camped nation. Ellicott cites Bishop Wordsworth: these words “pre-announced the blessed time of rest and peace, when God would abide with His Church on earth, by the gift of the Holy Ghost, and will tabernacle for ever with His people in heavenly rest and joy” (cf. Rev 7:15; 21:3). Guzik notes a tragic irony: “Moses prays that all God’s enemies will be scattered: the spies declare Israel will be defeated (Num 13). This chapter’s triumphant conclusion deepens the poignant tragedy of the succeeding scenes” (Wenham).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-10/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm

---

## Tradition-Specific Readings

I was unable to search comprehensively across all tradition-specific sites (Ligonier, Desiring God, GTY, Seedbed, LCMS, 1517.org, Catholic/Orthodox sites, NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey) due to search limits. However, some tradition-specific nuances do appear in the sources accessed:

- **Reformed/Baptist (Gill):** Gill reads the trumpets christologically – the Gospel ministry is the antitype. He sees the trumpets over sacrifices as expressing “joy for the acceptance of them, and especially when they had, by faith, a view of the great sacrifice of Christ typified by them.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-10.html)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik/Enduring Word):** Guzik emphasizes the parallel between trumpets and Spirit-empowered preaching, and connects the trumpet sound to the rapture (1 Thess 4:16–18) and the last trumpet (1 Cor 15:51–52). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-10/)

- **Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott stresses the liturgical and ecclesiastical applications – the trumpets point to the Gospel ministry, the Hobab invitation models the Church’s duty to invite others, and the march prayers prefigure the Spirit’s indwelling and heavenly rest. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/10.htm)

- **Older Broad Evangelical (Pulpit):** Notes the elasticity of Divine commands and adaptation under experience – e.g., the modification of the marching order (Gershonites and Merarites going ahead). Also emphasizes that the “ordinance forever” of the trumpets is perpetuated in the gospel. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/10.htm)

- **Methodist/Holiness (Henry):** Matthew Henry, though widely used across traditions, has a Wesleyan heritage. He emphasizes that sharing in Israel’s hardships leads to sharing in their comforts, and that “we can give only what we receive” – reflecting a theology of dependence on grace. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-10.html)

---
